content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore the properties of water, its different states, and its uses in everyday life. The focus area supports students to investigate the properties of solutions and solve problems to produce clean water.

Key ideas

  • The 3 states of water and their uses
  • Properties of water (boiling point, solvency, buoyancy)
  • Solutions as a type of liquid mixture
  • Solubility
  • Dilute and concentrated solutions
  • How to make clean water using separation techniques

Key terms

  • Solid, liquid, gas
  • Solution
  • Mixture
  • Soluble
  • Dilute, concentrated
  • Separation techniques (filtration, decantation, evaporation)
  • Buoyancy

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills in participating in planning and following scientific investigations related to solutions and mixtures. Students may develop skills in identifying problems, such as impure or dirty water, or substances that do not easily dissolve or float, and may participate in developing solutions to these problems.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Making predictions based on observations, such as ‘Which substance will dissolve or float in water?’ or ‘What will happen to ice or water as it is heated?’

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Measuring the change in temperature of water as it is heated.
  • Investigating which substances do and do not dissolve in water, such as salt and oil, after following a visual task analysis of steps, such as a video model, flow chart or procedural text.
  • Dissolving different solutes, such as coffee, tea, salt, sugar or jelly crystals, in cold and hot water after following a task analysis of steps.
  • Suggesting strategies to dissolve substances, such as using hot water or stirring.
  • Measuring, using least-to-most prompting hierarchy, the recommended quantity of cordial concentrate to form an appropriately diluted solution.
  • Recounting the innovative ways Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use water in the natural environment, by pointing on a communication board, choosing from binary choice or example/non-example prompts.
  • Classifying familiar substances, such as cordial or milk, as mixtures or pure substances by using a graphic organiser or concrete objects.
  • Demonstrating the process of cleaning polluted water using visual or verbal prompts.
  • Demonstrating a step in the separation techniques of filtration, decantation and evaporation, to clean dirty water.
  • Creating a beverage menu with recipes of different water-based hot and cold drinks.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to compare water obtained from different sources. Students could identify a question related to the quality of water in their local area, such as ‘Which is the cleanest water source: rainwater, sea water, grey water, bottled water, tap water or river water?’ A series of practical or secondary-sourced investigations designed to answer this question could be conducted using senses of sight, smell, taste (where safe to do so) and scientific tools to measure the turbidity, pH, or amount of trapped solids collected by a filter. Students may document the findings using photographs, diagrams, recordings, field notes, tables or charts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area introduces students to the physical properties of the 3 states of matter with a specific focus on the properties of water. Students learn to distinguish between atoms, mixtures and compounds and how the different types of mixtures can be separated based on their physical properties.

Key ideas

  • Water can be found as a solid, liquid and gas
  • Density
  • SI units of measurement
  • Solute, solvent and solution
  • Properties of solutions
  • Classifying matter as pure substances (compounds) and impure substances (mixtures)
  • Particle theory of matter
  • Separating mixtures using physical properties

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to observe different chemistry phenomena by planning and conducting a number of practical investigations. Students should also be given the opportunity to use their knowledge in problem-solving by identifying different solutions and strategies.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • planning an investigation to identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables when investigating the change in temperature of water as it is heated; the solubility of different substances; and the different methods used to separate mixtures
  • planning an investigation to understand the steps used to manage safety risks before, during and after an investigation
  • identify the methods and equipment needed when investigating the different methods used to separate mixtures
  • suggesting possible improvements to an investigation
  • conducting an investigation by selecting and/or assembling the correct equipment and following a planned procedure
  • processing data collected as part of investigations into density
  • analysing calculated density data and comparing it to SI units of measurement outlined in the  Science 7–10 Data Book
  • recording observations and measurements accurately during investigations.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise these concepts:

  • Practice of science using Working scientifically processes, by conducting an investigation using scientific tools and tabulating and graphing data from an investigation.
  • All objects are made of materials which have certain properties.
  • The properties of materials affect how they are used.
  • Water can exist as a solid, liquid or gas.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Measure the temperature as ice melts or water evaporates over a period of time.
  • Compare the density of water to other substances.
  • Investigate what substances are soluble in water.
  • Investigate the solubility of different solutes.
  • Investigate how temperature affects solubility.
  • Investigate the effect of salt on boiling point – 5% w/w, 10% w/w, 20% w/w, 30% w/w.
  • Investigate how to separate different types of mixtures.
  • Identify the cause-and-effect relationships involved in the cleaning of polluted water.

In context

Students model how a body of water can be polluted and then plan and conduct a practical investigation to ‘clean’ the water they have polluted. For example, students could add small pieces of plastic to represent rubbish pollution, vinegar to represent acid rain, or dirt to represent land clearing and then plan an investigation to separate some of the pollutants. This could be an opportunity for students to produce a scientific report, newspaper article or presentation on how to remove or prevent pollutants in a body of water.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds to produce a report or article, or the opportunity to plan and discuss their presentation using their home language or dialect.

This is a good opportunity for the students to learn how to conduct a second-hand research activity after researching their local water catchment area and identifying where that water comes from. Additionally, students could research what factors could contribute to a body of water becoming polluted and how that could be prevented.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate the effect of temperature on how much solute can be dissolved in water to make supersaturated solutions.
  • Investigate how solutions are used in everyday products. This can be expanded to look at the growing market of cleaning solutions that are made into solids to decrease the use of plastic consumption.
  • Investigate how an understanding of separating of mixtures is used in the dairy industry to make butter, buttermilk or cottage cheese.
  • Research how blood can be separated to make plasma, red blood cell and platelet transfusions, and why these 3 methods have been developed.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to investigate the features of plants and animals and explore how living things with similar features can be grouped together. Students have the opportunity to explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples classify plants and animals. The focus area supports students to communicate scientifically by describing features in detail, and sorting and grouping living things and everyday items.

Key ideas

  • Features of living things
  • Aboriginal Peoples’ Knowledge of the features of plants and animals
  • Classification of plants and animals
  • Vertebrates and invertebrates
  • Aboriginal Peoples’ ways of classifying plants and animals
  • Features of a cell

Key terms

  • Classify
  • Features
  • Observable
  • Vertebrates
  • Invertebrates
  • Cell

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills using scientific tools and their senses to observe the details of living things and communicate their understanding through various means, including written text.

The following additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Collecting and recording data from observations about features of living things.
  • Recognising patterns in the collected data in relation to the classification of living things.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Classifying real objects or representations of real objects, such as pictures, tactile cards or audio recordings, according to a given feature, such as colour, size, texture or sound.
  • Identifying different classifications of plants or animals in the local community, using one or more senses. For example, identifying flowering and non-flowering plants, shrubs or trees by looking at the plant to observe its height, feeling the features of the plant, such as its leaves or flowers, or by listening to an audio description of the plant. Important: ensure safety protocols are followed to avoid injuries, such as sunburn, cuts or insect bites, and that plants or animals are safe to be handled.
  • Engaging with local Aboriginal Elders or Cultural Knowledge holders to learn about how Aboriginal Peoples classify plants and animals, for example based on their edible or medicinal properties or other functional purposes.
  • Exploring parts of a cell by watching a video description or engaging with tactile models.
  • Exploring the features used to classify everyday objects and communicating the findings. For example, creating a graph of different materials in the classroom based on the sounds they make, their textures and their uses.
  • Exploring the benefits of classifying items in everyday life. For example, classifying different types of clothing allows students to neatly store and easily locate their belongings in a wardrobe, or classifying types of food on a shopping list makes it easier to locate items in a supermarket.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to identify different types of classification in a local area, recording and communicating their findings in a journal, scrapbook or photo. Students may observe how objects, animals or plants are classified using the senses, such as sight, touch, hearing, taste and smell, and where it is safe to do so. Students could communicate their ideas with others using a graph, tactile objects, a verbal description or a written paragraph.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to observe change in their everyday contexts, including chemical and geological change, and explore the role of energy in these changes. Students may engage with cultural accounts from local Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Communities and have opportunities to investigate features and changes to the local area. The focus area supports students to practise safe behaviours around energy sources and in the case of a fire.

Key ideas

  • Energy transfer
  • Roles of energy
  • Movement of energy
  • Safety around energy sources
  • Chemical change
  • Geological change

Key terms

  • Chemical change
  • Geological change
  • Energy
  • Energy transfer
  • Melting, boiling and evaporation
  • Conduction, convection and radiation
  • Fire
  • Landform

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills using scientific tools and their senses to observe examples of chemical and geological change. Students may develop skills in planning and safely participating in investigations of changes in everyday contexts.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as.

  • Communicating scientific information about chemical or geological changes in a variety of forms, such as photo collage, timelines, a verbal description, or via augmentation and alternative communication (AAC) devices.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing a range of changes, for example plant growth, weather or cooking, that occur in students’ everyday lives, using the senses, online resources, and audio or visual recordings.
  • Identifying and demonstrating the safe use of heating equipment, such as a microwave, stove or Bunsen burner. For example, picking up hot containers with tongs or mitts, or using the appropriate flame level to melt chocolate.
  • Exploring how heat is transferred through solids, liquids and gases as either conduction, convection or radiation. For example, placing a range of solids or liquids near a candle flame and measuring the differences in temperature over time using the senses, where safe to do so, or with scientific tools.
  • Following a sequence to mix 2 common household items, for example vinegar and baking soda, or baking soda and lemon juice, and observing the reaction using sight, sound or touch. Important: ensure chemicals are safe to be mixed before attempting with students. For example, mixing vinegar and bleach produces toxic gas.
  • Participating in planning an investigation to observe how erosion changes the landscape over time. For example, by pouring water over a mound of sand to simulate water erosion, or aiming a fan at a mound of sand to simulate wind erosion.
  • Exploring Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ stories of volcanoes, such as the Gunditjmara People’s tale of the Budj Bim volcano or the Gugu Badhun People’s tale of the Kinrara volcano, and the Mer tribes’ story of Apinini and Sidipuar.
  • Observing in person or virtually a site with different landforms, such as the Blue Mountains, using sight, sound, or touch.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to observe chemical changes that occur in cooking. They could participate in planning and safely preparing simple meals that show chemical change, such as frying an egg, baking bread, caramelising fruit or popping popcorn. Students could observe the changes, using their senses where safe to do so. Important: do not give students any food products they are allergic to. They may document the changes using a time lapse video, photo collage or written log.

This focus area aligns with the Stage 4 focus area, Data Science 1 and the Stage 5 focus area, Data Science 2.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore data and information used in everyday contexts, such as nutritional information, weather data and public transport timetables, and to engage with the ways in which scientists use data to make predictions or claims. The focus area supports students to make informed decisions in everyday contexts.

Key ideas

  • The nature of data
  • Privacy considerations when sharing personal information
  • Various ways to collect and organise data
  • Trends or patterns in data
  • Predictions based on available data
  • Scientific data
  • Making claims

Key terms

  • Data, dataset, trend, pattern
  • Evidence, claim, false claim
  • Privacy considerations

Skills

In this focus area, there are opportunities for students to record, organise and interpret data. Students may develop skills to make predictions and investigate the validity of claims based on available data and evidence. Students could present an argument of their choice that is supported by data.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as.

  • Participating in an investigation by following a sequence to search for and select trustworthy information.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Identifying information in everyday contexts, such as today's date and weather, or a room change.
  • Participating in collecting data, with the aid of scaffolded supports, such as participating in research; selecting relevant information from text, audio resources, videos or infographics; or participating in an investigation to collect data through a survey.
  • Organising and displaying data using visual, audio or tactile methods.
  • Observing patterns in data and making a prediction using the process of binary choice, based on a trend, such as a repeating colour sequence, the temperature rising or falling, or a growth increase.
  • Use least-to-most prompting hierarchy to identify sources of credible information that are based on evidence, such as social media, newspapers, health posters or pamphlets at a medical centre, or government websites (eg CSIRO, BoM).
  • Exploring how scientists collect data through adapted texts, teacher read-alouds or videos.
  • Exploring how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples share data through the passing on of stories.
  • Identifying evidence to support a claim using highlighting, text summary or dot points.
  • Interpreting data to make their own informed decisions using guided prompts, such as ‘I noticed … I wonder …?’ or sentence stems, ‘The data says … so I will …’

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to research and promote an improvement in the local area, such as inclusive furniture or a healthy canteen menu, or to raise awareness about an issue, such as the loss of native flora and fauna. They could collect and organise relevant data to support their argument using tables, lists, picture charts or digital displays. Students may present their argument using a slideshow, infographic or a podcast. They may participate in a debate to engage with the views of others regarding their project.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to identify the causes and effects of disease, and develop knowledge about some ways to prevent disease, such as personal hygiene and safe food preparation and storage. It supports students in identifying credible sources from which to access information related to health and to engage with the local community to access local health information, and contribute to community health by demonstrating practices to prevent the spread of disease.

Key ideas

  • The effects of disease
  • Infectious and non-infectious diseases
  • Some microorganisms can cause disease
  • Safe food preparation and storage
  • Disease control and prevention
  • Credible sources

Key terms

  • Infectious, non-infectious
  • Pathogen, virus, bacteria
  • Food safety
  • Immune system
  • Hygiene

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to interpret data and information about infectious and non-infectious diseases to inform themselves about how to prevent the spread of disease. Students may develop skills in communicating their understanding of disease, and disease control and prevention to a local audience.

The following additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Asking questions based on observations, such as questions about food-handling practices to prevent the spread of disease.
  • Participating in planning safe investigations by participating in decision-making about where to source data and information related to health or disease, and identifying what personal information should not be shared with strangers or published online.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing the symptoms of different diseases using one or more senses. For example, students could look at photographs of people with conjunctivitis or touch tactile cards representing symptoms such as sandpaper for an itchy throat or bubble wrap for a rash.
  • Observing Petri dishes with visual or tactile representations of microorganisms. If students are to handle live bacteria then safety precautions must be followed, such as handwashing before and after handling Petri dishes, and wearing mask or gloves.
  • Engaging in a role-play to simulate the actions of the immune system. Students could be assigned roles of either white blood cells, antibodies or germs, or props could be used as an alternative.
  • Engaging with a range of informative materials about local healthcare services, such as brochures, recorded radio advertisements or Braille pamphlets, to determine where to access medical information.
  • Investigating a range of infectious diseases and how to prevent them from spreading.
  • Investigating personal hygiene practices demonstrated in everyday living. For example, washing hands before participating in food technology lessons, covering the mouth when coughing, using adaptive tools such as long-handled brushes to clean the dishes after eating, or using a communication device to inform a staff member of the need to blow your nose.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to explore common infectious diseases of their choice and how to prevent them from spreading. They could access a variety of information sources, such as scientific news articles, infographics and expert interviews, to identify and collect relevant information about infectious diseases and ways to control them. Students may communicate the disease prevention and control practices they have identified by designing a poster or information pamphlet, recording a radio community service announcement, filming a television advertisement using Key Word Sign or Auslan, or using a communication board to point to pictures, one at a time, of the steps required to control and prevent disease.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to investigate the sources and uses of energy, the differences between renewable and non-renewable energy sources, and the importance of reducing energy usage. It supports students to advocate for social issues, such as access to energy, use of renewable energy sources and efficient energy use. This focus area provides opportunities for students to develop skills in using electricity, staying safe around electricity and electrical devices, and making informed choices about energy use.

Key ideas

  • Sources of energy
  • Alternative energy
  • Sources of electricity
  • Uses of electrical energy
  • Energy efficiency
  • Electricity safety
  • Energy transformations
  • Electrical circuits

Key terms

  • Fossil fuels
  • Combustion
  • Alternative energy
  • Energy transformations
  • Energy usage
  • Circuits
  • Voltage
  • Current

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to observe the different types and sources of energy used in everyday contexts. Students may develop skills in investigating simple electrical circuits, and process data and information, such as energy efficiency and ways to be safe around electrical devices.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as.

  • Identifying problems and strategies to solve these problems, such as identifying the cost or environmental impact associated with energy usage, and participating in developing solutions, such as using less energy or using more efficient appliances.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing combustion by listening to a car engine turn on, feeling the radiant heat produced by a lit candle, smelling food being cooked, or watching a video of a campfire being lit then extinguished. Important: always take safety precautions with any activities involving combustion, fire or heat.
  • Observing the effects of solar energy by placing a container of water in direct sunlight, then comparing the temperature change over time to that of a container of water kept in the dark. Temperature could be measured through touch, or a visual or talking thermometer.
  • Exploring energy transformation by rubbing hands together vigorously to feel the warmth generated, dropping a ball from different heights, switching a torch on and off, or playing a xylophone.
  • Demonstrating safe use of a range of electrical appliances, such as gaming consoles, kitchen appliances or fairy lights.
  • Investigating how to put the pieces of a circuit kit together to power simple appliances. For example, turning on a light bulb, spinning a fan or ringing an alarm.
  • Investigating the price and energy rating of a range of identified appliances then using this data to make a decision about an energy-efficient item that suits a given budget.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate ways to reduce personal energy usage and communicate this to their peers. They could explore and record the energy consumption of different personal appliances and everyday activities. Students may interpret the data to propose ways in which they can reduce their personal energy usage, such as switching to an appliance with lower consumption, or walking or taking public transport to school instead of being driven. They could communicate their findings to educate others about ways to reduce energy consumption, by designing an informative poster, radio or television advertisement using their preferred communication form(s).

This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore the human use of resources and its impact on the environment. It supports students to contribute to sustainable practices in the community and to manage their personal resources.

Key ideas

  • Resources management
  • Sustainable and unsustainable practices
  • Aboriginal Peoples’ resource management and sustainability
  • Managing resources used in daily living
  • Human impacts on the environment
  • Alternative resource use and recycling

Key terms

  • Sustainability, resource management
  • Climate change
  • Recycling
  • Alternative resource use

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to make predictions based on cause and effect that are related to the use of personal resources and the impact of human activities on the environment. Students may interpret information about human impact on climate and the environment to identify possible resource management strategies to improve sustainability in the local area.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Communicating strategies – using preferred communication form(s) – to improve sustainability, such as ways to manage personal resources, or ideas, such as how to reduce waste generation.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Predicting what would happen if resources were exhausted, such as a person consuming all their food for the day in the morning or using up their phone’s battery before lunch time.
  • Identifying ways to manage the day’s resources, such as portioning food in advance or dividing their lunch money between breaks.
  • Planting, harvesting and maintaining a vegetable garden to grow produce to be used in cooking lessons, and then composting the scraps for fertiliser in the garden.
  • Engaging with local Aboriginal Elders, Community members or local Landcare groups to explore how sustainable practices benefit all, such as cool burning, sustainable hunting, fishing and agricultural practices.
  • Interpreting symbols and information on packaging and containers to determine which items can be recycled and which cannot.
  • Participating in recycling, such as upcycling a plastic bottle or starting a worm farm.
  • Identifying the materials contained in everyday items by investigating product information or observing a product with their senses, such as touch, sight or smell, where safe to do so.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study through science or sustainability activities in their local area. They could investigate a range of activities by engaging with credible sources of information about current citizen science, or community environmental projects or campaigns. Students could select other relevant information, such as the objective and location of activity, and how much time they are able to commit. They could decide on an activity to participate in, based on personal interest and availability. Alternatively, students may start their own initiative by observing problem practices and identifying strategies to improve sustainability in their local area.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to recognise and investigate forces in everyday contexts. It supports students to use numbers and measurement to describe forces and develop problem-solving skills through investigating forces and applying this knowledge in designing or creating simple machines.

Key ideas

  • Scientific predictions
  • Forces
  • Friction
  • Gravity
  • Properties of magnets
  • Simple machines (lever, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, pulley, incline plane)

Key terms

  • Gravity
  • Friction
  • Magnetism

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills using their senses and scientific tools to make observations about forces and their applications in everyday contexts. Students may develop skills in asking questions and making predictions about the effects of forces on different objects.

The following additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Identifying problems and strategies to solve problems related to forces – aided by least-to-most prompting hierarchy, tactile models, visual display boards – to transfer skills and understanding of forces to practical everyday contexts. These contexts may include the uses of magnets, and the need to consider the dangers of placing equipment in high places and the hazards associated with slips, trips and falls in everyday contexts.
  • Interpreting investigation procedures by following a visual task analysis procedure or video model.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Predicting what will happen when students open and close doors, twist a wet towel, squeeze a lemon, or stretch an elastic band.
  • Observing how objects are affected by equal and unequal forces, such as pushing and pulling a trolley, as opposed to touching the trolley.
  • Observing how objects are affected by friction by examining the soles of shoes or a tyre of a bicycle.
  • Investigating how friction affects an object’s movement by sliding objects down oily, rough, wet, and dry surfaces.
  • Investigating everyday forces and communicating cause-and-effect using guided prompts, such as ‘I noticed ...’, ‘I wonder…?’ or sentence stems, such as ‘If I ... then ...’. For example: ‘I noticed when I pulled the rope the ball came towards me. I wonder what might happen if I kick the ball?’ or ‘If I push the skateboard down the ramp, then it will roll down and away from me.’
  • Investigating forces using different types of forces in the kitchen, such as cutting or squeezing oranges, or stirring, beating, pouring liquids and using a knife for spreading.
  • Investigating gravity by recording objects being dropped from different heights using a stopwatch, timer, audio recording or time-lapse video.
  • Investigating properties of magnets by engaging in their common usage, such as handling magnetic construction toys or fridge magnets by using the senses to observe and feel attraction and repulsion forces.
  • Demonstrating the attraction and repulsion properties of magnets by putting different poles of a magnet near metal objects.
  • Relating simple machines, such as levers, pulleys and inclined planes, to their authentic uses by observing and investigating everyday objects, such as a bicycle (pedals, chain, wheels), play equipment in a park, a bottle opener.
  • Investigating forces and simple machines made and used by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, such as woomeras, stone tools, grinding stones, and fire making tools (flints and fire drills) through demonstration by local Elders or approved Knowledge holders.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate how a variety of simple machines apply forces. The direction of force could be indicated using drawings, demonstrations, visual choice boards or gestures. Students may participate in applying the information they have collected to design and construct their own functioning models, such as a model car, that incorporate the concept of forces.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to observe living things, and examine closely the parts of plants and animals and the environment in which these things live. The focus area supports students to care for their own physical health and responsibly care for plants and animals.

Key ideas

  • Living and non-living things
  • The needs of living things
  • Caring for living things
  • Body parts and their functions
  • Keeping healthy
  • Parts of plants and their functions
  • Systems
  • Parts of ecosystems and their functions
  • Food chains and food webs
  • Environmental changes

Key terms

  • Living, non-living
  • Organs, body systems
  • Ecosystem
  • Food webs, food chains
  • Producers, consumers, decomposers
  • Energy

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills in asking questions and making predictions through the observation of living systems. Students may develop skills in interpreting data and information about the features and function of parts of plants and animals, or the needs of plants and animals.

The following additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Recording and organising data and information about living and non-living things in the local area
  • Recording the names of body parts using labels
  • Using scientific tools to make observations about living things.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing and identifying – using specimens, models or diagrams where appropriate – the features and functions of living things, body parts, body systems, plants and ecosystems, using one or more of their senses.
  • Exploring the local area and recording examples of living and non-living things, such as by drawing, taking photographs, using a voice recorder, writing a list, or using eye gaze to make observations.
  • Engaging in multisensory stories to explore body parts, systems and their functions. For example, textured materials can be used to represent different organs; sounds or auditory recordings can be played for body processes, such as a heart beating; and movement activities can be used to simulate processes, such as breathing.
  • Dissecting a flower to explore its features using sight, touch or smell.
  • Exploring through role-playing, storytelling, or puppetry how the different organisms in a food chain or food web interact with one another, and predicting what would happen if one or some organisms were removed.
  • Identifying what types of animals can be kept as pets.
  • Investigating how to care for pets using credible sources, such as RSPCA, local councils or local animal shelters, and developing an informative brochure or audio guide with pet care instructions.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate the effect of a relevant variable, such as soil, water or light, on the rate of plant growth. Students may make predictions on how plants would respond to changes in the identified variables. Students could measure the height of the plant over time using photographs or measuring tools, such as a ruler or Braille measuring tape, or observe growth through an augmented reality app. The data could be interpreted to determine whether the predictions were supported. Students may communicate their findings through delivering a show and tell, designing a visual communication board, or writing an instruction manual for optimising plant growth.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to identify resources in their everyday lives and develop understanding of the uses of plastics and their environmental impact. It supports students to value the Knowledges and practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples who use different kinds of resources and materials. The focus area supports students to make independent choices through planning and conducting investigations to identify possible solutions to reduce plastic waste in the local area.

Key ideas

  • Renewable and non-renewable resources
  • Managing personal resources
  • Sustainability
  • Uses of plastics
  • Environmental impacts of resource use
  • Managing environmental impacts

Key terms

  • Renewable, non-renewable
  • Sustainable
  • Environmental impact

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to participate in planning safe investigations to identify uses of renewable and non-renewable resources in everyday contexts and the impacts of plastics on the environment. Students may also develop skills in identifying problems with single-use plastic materials and strategies to reduce plastic usage or plastic littering in the local area.

The following additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Making predictions based on observations, such as ‘If I use my own cup instead of a plastic cup will it produce more or less waste?’, ‘Will changing the type of food packaging produce more or less waste?’, ‘Will placing a bin near the shop result in more or less littering?’
  • Asking questions based on observations of the use of materials in the local area, such as ‘Is there a way to reduce plastic littering near the local shop?’, ‘What can I do to reduce my own use of plastic?’

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Recording resources used in everyday contexts by writing or typing up a list, taking photographs, using dictation software, or using a communication device.
  • Classifying resources as renewable or non-renewable by sorting photographs or tactile cards into separate categories.
  • Identifying where resources are being wasted locally, such as leaking taps, dishwashers being used when not full, or hoses being used to clean outdoor surfaces instead of a broom.
  • Engaging with local Aboriginal Elders and Community members to investigate renewable resources that can be used as an alternative to plastics. For example, plant fibres can be woven to make baskets, natural resins can be used to seal containers, and clay or mud can be moulded into vessels and cooking pots.
  • Investigating why plastic litter is harmful to the environment by engaging with infographics, documentaries or local sustainability groups.
  • Describing the impacts of plastic in the environment by using augmented and alternative communication (AAC) devices, designing a poster or making a podcast.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate the amount of plastic litter in the local community. They could select an area of land and record plastic litter by taking photographs or indicating plastic waste for others to record, or by collecting, counting the number of, or weighing plastic items. Important: ensure safety protocols are in place, including the wearing of gloves and close supervision of all students. Students may use their findings to identify strategies to reduce plastic waste in the local area, such as packing lunch in reusable containers instead of single-use containers, running an education campaign with staff, students, residents or community members, or participating in, or organising, clean-up events.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore the nature and practice of science by making observations using one or more of their senses, and scientific tools and equipment. Students may collaborate with their peers and engage with the work practices of scientists and local Aboriginal Communities. This focus area supports students to identify and follow safe work practices, including identifying hazards and using equipment safely.

Key ideas

  • Uses of science
  • Making observations
  • Scientific equipment
  • Safety rules
  • Collaboration in science
  • Collecting and recording data
  • The Solar System

Key terms

  • Observation
  • Scientific equipment
  • Laboratory
  • Scientist
  • Working scientifically processes
  • Hazard

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills using their senses and scientific tools to make observations about the Universe. Students may develop skills in following a sequence to conduct scientific investigations and recording the results in different formats.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Participating in the planning of safe investigations by selecting appropriate scientific tools and instruments for investigations and participating in sequencing the steps in an investigation.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Making observations of the environment, such as listening to the sounds different materials make when tapped, or comparing under-watered and well-watered soil using sight and touch. Important: appropriate safety equipment must be used, such as gloves, sunscreen and safety goggles.
  • Engaging with Aboriginal Communities when making observations of the local environment and culturally significant sites.
  • Engaging with local Aboriginal Elders or Aboriginal Community members to learn how Aboriginal Peoples have gathered Knowledge about the Solar System over the millennia. Examples of engagement activities include: experiencing traditional stories or songs, such as Dreaming stories; creating star maps based on Songlines; exploring and analysing traditional rock art and engravings.
  • Investigating how to use equipment safely and following a sequence of steps to achieve licensing credentials for the use of scientific tools and equipment.
  • Investigating the types of plants, animals or vehicles in the local area, and recording observations using photographs, digital voice recorders, picture graphs, video documentation, switch-activated keyboards or electronic data loggers.
  • Investigating features of the Solar System by engaging with models or multimedia.
  • Investigating local weather and collecting related information using scientific tools, such as thermometers, rain gauges, weathervanes, talking thermometers, smartphone apps, tactile weather maps, wind chimes and kites.
  • Investigating hazards in the classroom or local area, including sharp edges, slippery surfaces and heavy or fragile objects.
  • Investigating ways to minimise or eliminate hazards in the environment, such as putting up ‘wet floor’ signs or notifying responsible persons of broken glass.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to identify types of graphs used to communicate scientific findings. They may investigate the types of graphs used to communicate local weather information, such as the current wind direction, the temperature change over a day, and the amount of rainfall in a month. They could further investigate a range of graph types and describe their features.

This focus area aligns with the Stage 5 focus area, Genetics and Evolutionary Change.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore through observation the physical traits of plants and animals that may be passed on genetically, and to examine their own personal genetic traits. Students have the opportunity to examine fossil evidence that shows small changes to the features of plants and animals over long periods of time as a result of evolution. The focus area supports students to develop self-awareness by considering their physical, genetic and acquired traits and to practise obtaining consent by asking permission to observe others’ traits.

Key ideas

  • Genetic and acquired traits
  • Evolutionary change
  • Consent

Key terms

  • Genetic
  • Evolution
  • Adaptation
  • Life cycle

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills using scientific tools and their senses to observe features of animals and plants, and the physical and acquired traits of humans. Students may record these features and traits using concrete materials, diagrams, photographs, audio recordings, lists, tables or charts. In this focus area students may communicate, using their preferred communication form(s), how they gained an acquired trait.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area.

  • Asking questions based on their observations of features of plants and animals, such as ‘Why do kangaroos have a pouch?’, ‘What does fur do for an animal?’, ‘How do animals learn?’

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing their personal genetic traits using senses and scientific tools, such as: measuring their height with a tactile tape measure; observing their eye colour by using a mirror, Braille or tactile photographs, or by receiving descriptions from familiar people; feeling or looking at their earlobes to determine if they are long or short; or measuring or feeling the length of their toes.
  • Classifying examples of genetic and acquired traits, for example by making lists, sorting photographic or tactile representations, or using an augmentative and alternative communication device (AAC).
  • Observing plants and animals and their offspring by viewing photographs, diagrams or videos, by listening to an audio description, or by touching tactile cards that identify similar features between generations.
  • Collecting and recording personal and family genetic information, such as by writing in a notebook, recording an audio log, or compiling a selection of photographs. Before using recordings, images or names of deceased Indigenous persons, seek guidance from local Elders or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community members.
  • Identifying features of animals that help them survive in different environments, such as fins for swimming, fur to control body temperature, and sharp teeth to hunt prey.
  • Engaging with fossil evidence of plants and animals, such as rock fossils, videos or tactile models to identify features that existed in the distant past.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students could participate in a depth study and collaborate with their peers to record their personal traits, such as eye colour, hair colour or height, using any preferred methods, such as tally sheets, graphs, Braille notes or audio log. They may practise seeking consent to observe and record others’ traits by using an AAC device or seeking written or verbal permission. Students could select the most appropriate measuring tools for different types of measurement, such as a tactile tape measure, a ruler or digital devices.

This focus area aligns with the Stage 4 focus area, Periodic Table and Atomic Structure.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to classify materials according to their properties, including the classification of familiar objects, materials and substances as solids, liquids or gases; metals or non-metals; and flammable, combustible, toxic or corrosive. It supports students to identify and safely use potentially hazardous materials and chemicals.

Key ideas

  • States of matter
  • Properties of metals and non-metals
  • Uses of metals
  • Hazardous materials and chemicals
  • Warning symbols and labels
  • Safe storage of hazardous chemicals
  • First aid for exposure to hazardous chemicals

Key terms

  • Solids, liquids and gases
  • Metals and non-metals
  • Chemical property
  • Chemical exposure
  • Toxic chemical
  • Flammable, combustible, toxic, corrosive
  • First aid

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills in recording information related to objects, materials and substances. Students may develop skills in interpreting labels and symbols to identify the properties and toxicity of household chemicals and how to provide first aid for chemical exposure.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Identifying problems and strategies that can be used to solve them such as identifying a range of hazards in the home or local area, and participating in developing solutions, such as designing or applying warning labels, signage or educational resources to promote safe practices.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Exploring objects in everyday contexts, such as water, ice cube, an inflated balloon or steam from soup, using the senses where safe to do so, to identify whether they are solids, liquids or gases.
  • Conducting an experiment to sort metals and non-metals into groups, based on one or more features, and recording the results. For example, sorting metals and non-metals according to whether they corrode or conduct heat. Important: Ensure students stay safe while working with corrosive substances or heat by wearing the appropriate safety equipment such as goggles and/or gloves.
  • Interpreting labels on household chemicals using sight, Braille labels or AAC devices. Important: Do not allow students to handle toxic chemicals without safety precautions.
  • Engaging with Aboriginal Elders or Aboriginal Community members to experience local natural resources that can be used in healing practices. Students could observe tea tree leaves being crushed or boiled to extract essential oil, feel the texture of paperbark which can be used as a wound dressing, or smell eucalyptus which can be used to alleviate respiratory symptoms.
  • Demonstrating how to correctly store toxic chemicals.
  • Identifying appropriate warning signs and labels using pictures, Braille or audio that are used to alert people of the dangers associated with toxic chemicals.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to identify examples of toxic chemicals found in the home by producing a list, taking photographs or indicating toxic chemicals in a picture of a kitchen cabinet. Alternatively, photos of common household chemicals or tactile warning symbols could be used instead. Ensure safety protocols are in place and that they are communicated to families if this is an activity students will be doing at home. Students may interpret the warning labels on the chemicals they identified in order to outline the appropriate handling and storage of these chemicals, and how to administer first aid in the case of exposure.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to safely observe and describe chemical reactions, as well as supporting them to work safely with chemicals and collaborate in planning and conducting scientific investigations involving chemical reactions. It supports students to apply their learning in everyday contexts by investigating ways to prevent rust and ways to dissolve substances quickly.

Key ideas

  • Identifying chemical reactions
  • Describing chemical reactions
  • Chemical reactions can be fast or slow
  • Dangerous chemical reactions
  • Effects of temperature on chemical reactions

Key terms

  • Chemical reaction
  • Combustion
  • Corrosion
  • Dissolution
  • Particle

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to participate in planning safe investigations to observe chemical reactions. Students may develop skills in identifying solutions to problems, such as reducing the temperature to make a chemical reaction slower and less dangerous, or crushing a tablet to make it dissolve faster.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Communicating ideas about chemical reactions by written text, using language appropriate to purpose and audience.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Observing changes in everyday chemical reactions, such as a candle burning or a metal rusting. Observing the candle could include noticing the light and heat produced, the wax melting, the candle size decreasing, the black soot on a surface placed over the candle. Observing the metal could include noticing changes in colour, lustre and texture. Important: taking safety precautions such as using appropriate goggles and gloves while observing chemical reactions or handling hot or sharp materials is essential.
  • Consulting with local Elders or approved Knowledge holders to investigate chemical reactions used in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander practices, such as crushing and rubbing the leaves of the red ash tree to make bush soap, using egg yolk as a natural glue to help seal painted surfaces, crushing Kakadu plum into a paste for face cream, and stunning fish using kangaroo apple.
  • Observing videos or listening to descriptions of chemical reactions, such as elephant’s toothpaste, or carbonated drink reactions.
  • Planning a safe investigation, such as testing the reaction of bi-carbonate of soda and vinegar by first viewing a video or listening to a description, then discussing safety protocols, such as conducting the experiment in an outdoor area to avoid spills and slipping, wearing safety goggles to prevent liquid splashing into their eyes, and changing the amount of vinegar to control the scale of the reaction.
  • Observing and timing a range of fast and slow chemical reactions using scientific tools or the senses, such as watching a live demonstration or video, or listening to audio descriptions.
  • Investigating how temperature affects reaction time by cooking an egg at different temperatures and measuring the cooking time.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate ways to prevent a metal from rusting. They could identify some ways to prevent a steel nail or screw from rusting in a salt-water solution, such as painting the metal, coating it in water, or changing the temperature of the water. Students may make predictions about the effect of each of these ideas. They could then participate in one or more experiments to determine the effectiveness of these strategies to reduce rusting. Important: ensure appropriate protective equipment is used when participating in experiments. Students may communicate their findings through written texts, such as writing bulleted sentences, a descriptive paragraph or a scientific report, or other preferred communication method(s).

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore the properties of water, its different states, and its uses in everyday life. The focus area supports students to investigate the properties of solutions and solve problems to produce clean water.

Key ideas

  • The 3 states of water and their uses
  • Properties of water (boiling point, solvency, buoyancy)
  • Solutions as a type of liquid mixture
  • Solubility
  • Dilute and concentrated solutions
  • How to make clean water using separation techniques

Key terms

  • Solid, liquid, gas
  • Solution
  • Mixture
  • Soluble
  • Dilute, concentrated
  • Separation techniques (filtration, decantation, evaporation)
  • Buoyancy

Skills

In this focus area there are opportunities for students to develop skills in participating in planning and following scientific investigations related to solutions and mixtures. Students may develop skills in identifying problems, such as impure or dirty water, or substances that do not easily dissolve or float, and may participate in developing solutions to these problems.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Making predictions based on observations, such as ‘Which substance will dissolve or float in water?’ or ‘What will happen to ice or water as it is heated?’

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Measuring the change in temperature of water as it is heated.
  • Investigating which substances do and do not dissolve in water, such as salt and oil, after following a visual task analysis of steps, such as a video model, flow chart or procedural text.
  • Dissolving different solutes, such as coffee, tea, salt, sugar or jelly crystals, in cold and hot water after following a task analysis of steps.
  • Suggesting strategies to dissolve substances, such as using hot water or stirring.
  • Measuring, using least-to-most prompting hierarchy, the recommended quantity of cordial concentrate to form an appropriately diluted solution.
  • Recounting the innovative ways Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use water in the natural environment, by pointing on a communication board, choosing from binary choice or example/non-example prompts.
  • Classifying familiar substances, such as cordial or milk, as mixtures or pure substances by using a graphic organiser or concrete objects.
  • Demonstrating the process of cleaning polluted water using visual or verbal prompts.
  • Demonstrating a step in the separation techniques of filtration, decantation and evaporation, to clean dirty water.
  • Creating a beverage menu with recipes of different water-based hot and cold drinks.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to compare water obtained from different sources. Students could identify a question related to the quality of water in their local area, such as ‘Which is the cleanest water source: rainwater, sea water, grey water, bottled water, tap water or river water?’ A series of practical or secondary-sourced investigations designed to answer this question could be conducted using senses of sight, smell, taste (where safe to do so) and scientific tools to measure the turbidity, pH, or amount of trapped solids collected by a filter. Students may document the findings using photographs, diagrams, recordings, field notes, tables or charts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides opportunities for students to investigate different types of waves and motion in everyday contexts. It supports students to model and describe waves and motion using numbers and measurements, verbal descriptions, and text and diagrams.

Key ideas

  • Waves
  • Sound waves occur due to vibration
  • Light waves
  • Light can be reflected
  • Motions of people and objects
  • Newton’s laws of motion

Key terms

  • Sound waves
  • Light waves
  • Vibration
  • Motion
  • Speed
  • Newton’s laws of motion

Skills

In this focus area, there are opportunities for students to safely participate in investigations about waves and the motion of objects. Students may record numbers and measurements associated with waves and motion, such as the time for a wave or object to travel from one point to another, or the distance travelled by a moving person or object. They may record features of waves or descriptions of motion using sound or video recording devices, diagrams, verbal descriptions or written text.

Additional skills may be developed in this focus area, such as:

  • Communicating data and information related to modelling motion and the reflection of light.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interests and further develop the targeted Working scientifically processes.

  • Modelling and observing wave motion by dropping an object into a body of water to observe the ripples, or plucking a guitar string to observe the vibrations.
  • Recording sounds in the local community using a digital recording device. Sounds could include insects, music, ambient noise or people talking. Important: ensure consent is obtained before recording other people.
  • Exploring how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples use waves and motion in tools, such as didgeridoos, clapping sticks, emu callers, woomeras or boomerangs.
  • Creating a ‘sound or listening’ bingo game with recorded sounds to match to images.
  • Observing the vibrations of objects when they produce sounds, such as feeling the vibration on a loudspeaker or drum.
  • Exploring common sources of light, such as a torch, the sun or a lit candle. Important: ensure safety precautions, such as not looking directly at the Sun and keeping a safe distance from a lit candle.
  • Modelling the reflection of light on different materials by shining a torch on different surfaces, such as a mirror, aluminium foil, or a piece of high gloss plastic.
  • Exploring the movements of everyday objects by recording motion using a time lapse video or noting the approximate location of an object by the sounds it makes. The motion could be modelled by placing dots on a tactile model, arranging arrows to show the direction, or representing fast and slow periods of motion on a sequenced time chart.
  • Observing the different ways people or objects move, such as a person jumping up and down or moving forwards and backwards, or a leaf fluttering in the wind.
  • Measuring and recording the distance and time travelled by a person, such as a student going to the canteen, or a teacher going to the staffroom.
  • Recording the time taken to get from point A to point B using a variety of motion styles, such as walking, running, skipping, crawling or rolling in a wheelchair.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. Content from the in-context content group may be a starting point for students to consider a depth study.

For example:

  • Students may participate in a depth study to investigate and model Newton’s laws of motion in everyday contexts. They may safely participate in experiments to explore the relationship between an object’s movements and the forces acting on it, such as the coin drop experiment where a piece of cardboard is pulled out from under a coin causing it to fall into a glass of water (demonstrating inertia), pushing shopping trolleys containing different amounts of goods, or inflating a balloon and attaching it to a string to create a balloon rocket.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area gives students opportunities to investigate the use of keys and classification systems to identify and describe organisms. Students also investigate the specialised structure and functions of cells and cell organelles, and describe the role and importance of specialised cells in multicellular organisms.

Key ideas

  • Classification systems
  • Adaptations
  • Dichotomous keys
  • Cell structures and organelles
  • Specialisation
  • Cellular respiration
  • Photosynthesis

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to observe and classify a variety of organisms using dichotomous keys and identify organisms using the Linnaean classification system. Students could develop their skills in observing, conducting investigations and communicating by using technologies to investigate cell specialisation and structures, and by making scientific diagrams and models.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • planning the investigation of species found in a local area
  • collecting data through a survey, recording the data in a table or spreadsheet, and analysing the data for patterns and trends.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise these concepts:

  • features of living things
  • grouping living things according to their external features
  • the structural adaptations living things have that support their survival.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Interpret dichotomous keys to classify a variety of organisms.
  • Survey of the local habitat using fieldwork, videos, images or field guides to identify native plant species and/or animals. Describe how organisms surveyed are adapted to their environment.
  • Make observations of cells and cell organelles using interactive online simulations, tactile models and microscopes.
  • Draw or collect images of single-celled organisms observed using a microscope.
  • Make a wet mount slide (eg onion cell, elodea, hay infusion, pond water) to observe and describe a variety of cells.
  • Compare similarities and differences between different types of cells, eg plant and animal cells, using images, tables, audio recordings or Venn diagrams.
  • Construct models to identify the process of photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
  • Model the process of diffusion and relate it to cellular respiration.

In context

Students research an organism to explain its classification and describe how classification encompasses all the characteristics of living things. Students could also research an Australian native animal (such as the platypus) and explain the features that lead scientists to classify it in a particular manner.

  • Kingdom: Animalia
  • Phylum: Chordata
  • Class: Mammalia
  • Order: Monotremata
  • Family: Ornithorhynchidae
  • Genus: Ornithorhynchus
  • Species: Ornithorhynchus anatinus

Students could apply their understanding of the characteristics of living things to explain the classification of the platypus. Examples could include what they eat, how they grow and how they respond to changes in the environment.

This could be a good opportunity for students to produce a field guide, scientific news article or scientific poster that would be useful to display in a zoo.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolding, and provision to use their home language or dialect or a bilingual dictionary to research and produce a scientific news article.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate a cellular process such as photosynthesis. Students pose questions, identify variables, and follow a planned procedure to make observations and draw evidence-based conclusions. Students document the process in the format of a procedural text.
  • Investigate the health of a local habitat such as a creek. Students identify organisms using keys, collect qualitative and quantitative observations about the biotic and abiotic features of the habitat, and identify adaptations that enable organisms to survive in this environment. Students could communicate with local groups such as Bushcare, NSW Waterwatch, local councils and Local Aboriginal Land Councils to evaluate their assessment of the health of the chosen habitat and discuss possible solutions and recommendations to maintain and/or improve the health and useability of the area.
  • Extend the concept of classification by investigating how the classification of a type of plant or animal has changed due to new discoveries or emerging technologies. Students could investigate how the light microscope led to the addition of other kingdoms such as Protista and Monera (bacteria).

In this focus area, students explore energy transfers (conduction, convection, radiation) and the distinctions between them. They learn about various energy storage systems such as thermal, elastic, chemical, and gravitational potential energy, and how energy transfers between these forms. In chemical change, students learn to identify physical and chemical change indicators and observe energy changes in reactions. In geological change, students learn about plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, and Aboriginal Peoples accounts of geological phenomena. They explore minerals, rocks, the rock cycle, fossil formation and the elemental composition of the Earth. Students develop a holistic understanding of the concept of change.

Key ideas

  • Forms of energy
  • Energy change
  • Types of heat transfer
  • Physical and chemical change
  • Scientific theories and laws
  • Geological processes
  • Fossil record

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to:

  • follow planned procedures and use scientific tools and instruments to make observations of energy transfers and transformations
  • conduct investigations to identify indicators that a chemical change has occurred
  • observe energy changes in a chemical reaction.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • questioning and predicting using models and simulations to investigate energy transformations, including the transformation of radiant energy into electrical energy
  • questioning and predicting using a variety of models to investigate change, including the rock cycle to model geological processes, formation of fossils and the law of superposition.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise these concepts.

  • Types of energy.
  • The effect of geological change on the Earth’s surface.
  • How matter and energy are cycled through a system.
  • Cellular processes.

Investigations

The following activities may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Undertake qualitative observations of convection currents in liquids, eg boiling rice, lava lamps.
  • Carry out quantitative observations of radiant energy heating materials, eg radiation cans, different coloured fabrics in the Sun.
  • Plan a valid investigation to collect qualitative and quantitative observations of energy transformations, eg bouncing a ball (gravitational, kinetic and elastic), observing elastic potential energy stored in a spring or elastic band, using solar panels to convert light energy into electrical energy.
  • Investigate the law of conservation of energy, eg energy transformations in a pendulum.
  • Make qualitative observations to compare the difference between physical and chemical changes, eg breaking a paddle pop stick into pieces versus burning it, malleability of magnesium ribbon versus burning magnesium.
  • Observe the conduction of heat through different materials, eg metals and insulators.
  • Investigate energy changes in chemical reactions using data loggers or thermometers to measure temperature changes, eg vinegar and bicarbonate of soda, handwarmers.
  • Use mineral kits to compare the observable properties of different types of minerals and rocks.
  • Use images and multimodal simulations to observe large-scale geological changes.
  • Investigate observations made that support the theory of plate tectonics.

In context

Students are required to observe or design a chain reaction machine. Students could design and construct a Rube Goldberg machine to represent energy stores and transfers within a complex system. Students could stack several dominoes vertically as a potential energy store.

Process: Attach a string to the top domino. At the top, place a small toy car on a small, inclined ramp. When the dominoes fall, they release potential energy, which is transferred to the toy car. The toy car accelerates down the ramp, converting the potential energy into kinetic energy. At the bottom of the ramp, the toy car collides with a wooden block, transferring its kinetic energy to the block.

Students could document the energy transfers as a factual description or descriptive report.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and explicit teaching of the language of description to produce a description or descriptive report.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate the chemical reaction between yeast and sugar (fermentation) to produce carbon dioxide. Observe the indicators of a chemical change (gas), and confirm the products produced. Investigate variables affecting fermentation such as temperature and type of sugar used and measure the amount of gas produced. 
  • Investigate the location of plate boundaries and volcanic activity.
  • Extend knowledge of chemical change to identify applications in daily living, eg exploring traditional bush foods and medicines (using soft bracken fern to treat insect bites).
