content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area provides an opportunity for students to broaden their understanding of how data is used in science, including development of scientific models, eg predicting movement of celestial objects and weather patterns. Students can also build on their problem-solving by proposing solutions and recognising data that supports or refutes identified predictions. Teachers can also broadly integrate this focus area with other focus areas.

Key ideas

  • Data science
  • Scientific achievements of Aboriginal people
  • Scientific models, including different types and their predictive power
  • Models of the Universe
  • Accuracy and reliability of primary data
  • Using statistics including mean and range to analyse data

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to explore how data can be analysed using simple descriptive statistics, including mean and range, and apply this to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of data collected. Analysed data can be used to identify possible strategies to solve identified problems.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • identifying investigable questions and making predictions using a dataset or through primary investigation.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Testable questions.
  • Predicting based on observation or evidence.
  • Processing numerical data.
  • Variables in scientific investigations.
  • Calculating mean and range.
  • Describing trends, patterns and relationships in data.
  • Scientific models and theories.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Conducting a practical investigation to collect a dataset, eg a survey of food preferences of a class or year group, fieldwork to observe and track changes in biotic and abiotic features such as vegetation type and distribution, temperature, moisture, and light intensity.
  • Engaging with relevant local groups such as the local council, Bushcare, Aboriginal Land Councils or national parks to identify issues such as pests and weeds, collect data, and propose solutions.
  • Analysing computer-generated models, eg weather modelling, predicting the path of asteroids, biodiversity and population models, including the use of these models to make predictions, and identifying the data that scientists used to generate these models.

In context

Students are required to create a model that can be used to explain an observable phenomenon, such as:

  • a simple machine to show how levers can be used as a force multiplier, eg trebuchet, pulleys and gears
  • a model of an organ or organ system to demonstrate its function
  • a model of the particles to demonstrate expansion and contraction in a familiar material such as an elastic hair band or a car tyre
  • a model of specific phenomena in our solar system, eg eclipses, predicted path of comets and asteroids, sunspots.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce an explanation through a written report, video or speech to identify strong cause-and-effect links. This is also an opportunity for students to develop their skills in evaluating an explanation and model against a provided rubric.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and explicit teaching of language features such as cause-and-effect and prediction to produce an explanation.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Develop questions that can be investigated either using a provided dataset or through first-hand investigation. For example, students could investigate the effect of soil salinity on germination or growth rates, the effectiveness of energy-efficient house designs, how ocean acidification affects shellfish or corals, whether warmer sea temperatures cause stronger cyclones.
  • Plan and conduct an investigation to identify and collect relevant data, process and analyse the data and draw evidence-based conclusions that address their identified question.
  • Use a dataset, investigate different ways that data can be presented, and assess how trends, patterns and relationships can be effectively communicated to a specific audience.
  • Investigate the achievements of Aboriginal scientists.
  • Extend understanding of models by investigating 2 competing theories that explain the origin of the universe, eg the Big Bang model and steady-state theory. Compare observations and evidence that support each model and explain why the model is accepted or rejected.

In this focus area, students explore the effects of direct and indirect forces, including gravity, electrostatic forces and magnetism. Students investigate the use of force diagrams, analyse the relationship between force and energy, and explore the practical applications of simple machines in everyday life, all within the context of forces and magnetism.

Key ideas

  • Scientific theories and laws
  • Direct and indirect forces
  • Balanced and unbalanced forces
  • Energy
  • Electrostatic, gravitational and magnetic forces
  • Simple machines

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to form questions about and make predictions regarding phenomena. Students should have the opportunity to follow a method and use scientific instruments to collect data which is then analysed in a variety of ways.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • questioning and predicting by formulating questions to investigate and making predictions about a possible outcome, such as investigating the relationship between mass and the force required to move a block across a surface
  • collecting quantitative data using scientific equipment
  • collecting qualitative data and drawing conclusions
  • conducting investigations (including those modelled by the teacher), processing and analysing data and sharing scientific findings using a chosen communication method.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • The movement of objects is dependent on forces.
  • How forces interact in a system to perform a function.
  • The effect of changing the amount of force on an object.
  • Magnets and objects that magnets will be attracted to.
  • The structure of the Earth.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Demonstrate the magnetic fields of bar magnets, horseshoe magnets and compasses, and their interactions using iron filings.
  • Investigate static electricity using charged rods (acrylic glass rod, silk, ebonite and wool) and pith balls.
  • Investigate static electricity by observing an electroscope or charging a balloon by rubbing it with cloth and trying to pick up small pieces of paper and/or feeling its effect on body hair.
  • Investigate friction using a spring balance to pull a mass across different types of surfaces, such as a carpet, tiles or a lab bench.
  • Compare calculated and measured mass using newton metres and digital scales.
  • Investigate the forces acting in Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ lives such as bow and arrow, tool sharpening or fire starting.
  • Construct and compare the strength of electromagnets by changing the core material or the number of turns in the wire coil and testing how many paperclips are picked up by the magnet.
  • Investigate the action of forces, such as: testing if the length of a lever arm affects the force required to lift an object; exploring how a pulley system can make lifting objects easier; or investigating how the angle of an inclined plane affects the force required to move an object uphill.
  • Investigate how simple machines can solve everyday issues such as using a spoon as a lever to open a jar lid.

In context

Students investigate forces and magnetism in familiar contexts. This may include areas such as transport (bikes), simple machines (levers), sports (football, cricket, softball) and toys (paper helicopters).

Students may present information through a written report, video, speech or demonstration on the effect of forces in everyday contexts. Students could investigate:

  • the nature of levers
  • pulley systems
  • designs to reduce the impact of friction
  • designs that rely on friction.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds to produce written reports and provision to plan and discuss their speech using their home language or dialect.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigating the effect of forces in toys or sport: students could investigate the nature of how forces act, how changing the nature of these forces (strength, direction) or the object (mass, friction) leads to different outcomes and how this relates to the desired outcome for the toy or sport.
  • Extending the concept of gears and how they work as simple machines: students could construct workable models of different-sized gears and investigate their use in real-world contexts.
  • Investigating complex machines: designing a complex machine out of as many simple machines as possible to solve a task.

This focus area allows students to develop their understanding of multicellular organisms and their interactions in an ecosystem. Students focus on the role of the digestive, circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems of humans, and the role of the xylem and phloem in multicellular plants.

Key ideas

  • Multicellular organisms have different systems
  • Movement of nutrients and waste in plants and animals
  • Disorders and their impact on a system
  • Ecosystems are determined by their abiotic and biotic factors
  • Food webs
  • Ecological food pyramids
  • Unique Australian species
  • Effect of introduced species
  • Interdependent role of systems
  • Matter and energy cycles in a system

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to develop their skills in researching information to make valid predictions, process data and information, and use appropriate models to communicates ideas.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • investigating human systems (eg digestive, circulatory, respiratory or excretory) using scientific knowledge of human systems to question and predict the effects of disorders to part of a system
  • extracting information from texts, diagrams or multimedia to identify and label images of cells
  • using models (eg food webs, pyramids, or carbon/oxygen/nitrogen/water cycles) to simplify and represent complex phenomena
  • presenting findings with relevant scientific terms and diagrams for a specific purpose and audience.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Living things change over time.
  • Living things require energy.
  • The balance of nutrients and organisms in an environment.
  • How physical conditions affect the survival of living things.
  • The conditions needed for a particular plant or animal to grow and survive.
  • How changing physical conditions in an environment affect the growth and survival of living things.
  • How the structural and behavioural features of living things support their survival.
  • Multicellular organisms are made up of a variety of specialised cells and tissues that support their needs.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Dissect plants to observe roots, flowers, stems and leaves.
  • Observe water movement in xylem and transpiration using a celery experiment.
  • Observe onion cells using microscopes with iodine or the tactile model.
  • Use stereo microscopes (×40) or diagrams for leaf, flower, root and stem examination.
  • Model local food webs and ecosystem matter/energy flows.
  • Research and compare different living systems and then predict what could happen if a part of that system is missing or damaged, eg the effect on an individual without an organ such as a kidney or a spleen, or the effect on a plant without its leaves, roots or flowers.
  • Investigate the influence of biotic and abiotic factors on organisms, such as how food availability (eucalyptus leaves) and climate (extreme temperature) interact to affect the distribution and health of koala populations in different parts of Australia.

In context

Students are required to investigate factors that have led to a species becoming endangered or extinct and explain why Australia has some of the world’s highest extinction rates. Each group of students could research one extinct or endangered animal, such as the Tasmanian tiger or the lesser bilby, and then develop a presentation such as a poster, video or report describing the factors that led to the endangerment or extinction of their chosen animal.

Students could then go on a mock ‘field trip’ through the class, moving between presentations to learn the reasons for each animal’s endangerment or extinction. Once all data has been collected, the class could work together to come up with explanations for Australia’s high extinction rates. Possible explanations might include geographical isolation or habitat destruction.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and provision to use their home language or dialect and a bilingual dictionary to research, plan and produce a presentation.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Comparing 2 different ecosystems by examining the abiotic and biotic features in each.
  • Comparing structural features of different plants in an ecosystem.
  • Investigating the history of organ transplants or possible future advances in this area.
  • Extending understanding of the impact of disease on a human body system, eg the impact of coeliac disease on the digestive system.

In this focus area, students explore the nature and practice of science as a set of processes used to observe and build a body of knowledge about the Universe and the world around us. Students should be encouraged to draw on observations relevant to their own lives, to develop questions about the world around them and to find answers to these questions by making observations using their senses, tools and technologies.

Key ideas

  • Observations and inferences
  • Qualitative and quantitative data
  • Conducting safe investigations
  • Variables
  • SI units of measurement
  • Positions of the planets in the Solar System
  • Relative positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to make observations using their senses and a variety of technologies and tools appropriate for scientific observation. Students should also have the opportunity to develop and demonstrate their competency in safely following planned procedures to record both qualitative and quantitative observations.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • questioning and predicting using observations and measurements to answer questions posed
  • planning investigations by seeking permission to use specialised equipment
  • justifying how equipment choice affects the accuracy and precision of the measurements
  • analysing data and information using either observations collected over a period of time or provided data to identify trends, patterns and relationships, and draw conclusions.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • The Earth is part of a system of planets orbiting around a star (the Sun).
  • Understanding of the Universe is developed by making observations and gathering data.
  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use observations of the night sky to inform decisions about resources and significant Cultural night sky and weather patterns.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Conduct a science mystery box experiment: objects are placed in sealed boxes and students make observations using their senses that may lead to inferences about the objects inside the boxes.
  • Use wire gauze to qualitatively determine the hottest part of the Bunsen burner flame.
  • Heat copper carbonate in a test tube to make qualitative observations and inferences.
  • Compare observations made using the senses to those made with technologies (compare visual, auditory or tactile observations of leaves, insects and flowers to observations made with digital photographs and recordings, bio viewers and microscope views, or electron micrograph images).
  • Use digital and analog thermometers to observe temperature changes during the day in shaded and unshaded areas.
  • Investigate insulation with water in aluminium cans by observing the effect of the colour of the insulating material on the temperature of can.
  • Investigate Dreaming stories of Aboriginal Peoples that are connected to the Universe.
  • Construct models to predict solar and lunar eclipses.

In context

Students investigate how a recent advancement in science has increased our knowledge of the world and the Universe. This could be an opportunity for students to engage with scientific media and produce a written text or podcast to discuss the importance of collaboration and multiple perspectives in the advancement of science, for example:

  • explore how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples' observations of the sky, the solar system and universe contributes to scientific knowledge.
  • scientific discoveries and advancements made possible by the collaboration of multiple agencies involved in running the International Space Station.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as pre-teaching vocabulary, scaffolds and provision to use home language or dialect to access scientific media and to produce persuasive texts.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • A series of observations or fieldwork in the local area related to student-developed questions.
  • Extending the concept of tropism – including gravitropism, phototropism and thigmotropism – by conducting research into the effect of either gravity, light, or mechanical touch on plant growth.

In this focus area, students develop a deeper understanding of matter, elements and atoms and what comprises them. Students learn how to use the periodic table to predict trends and patterns before investigating the availability, properties and uses of specific materials.

Key ideas

  • Elements and the periodic table
  • Subatomic particles – protons, neutrons and electrons
  • Physical properties of metals, metalloids and non-metals
  • Uses of elements, compounds and alloys
  • Atomic structure modelling
  • Atomic number
  • Element symbols

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • conducting an investigation to identify the physical properties of metals, non-metals and metalloids
  • modelling atomic structure by proton, neutron and electron numbers of the first 18 elements
  • processing and analysing data and information from texts, diagrams, flow charts and multimedia to identify the historical changes in the atomic structure
  • assessing the reliability of gathered data and information when researching, eg how technologies have helped shape our understanding of the model of the atom, or the elemental composition of the Earth compared to another planet
  • making predictions using identified patterns and relationships in the periodic table
  • proposing inferences based on presented data and information when investigating tests to identify metal and non-metal elements.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • All objects are made of materials which have certain properties.
  • The properties of materials affect their use.
  • The purpose of science is to build knowledge and understanding of the world.
  • Advancements in science are often the result of collaboration.
  • Matter can display different properties as a solid, liquid or gas.
  • Mixtures and pure substances have different properties.
  • Metals are used in the production of tools.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Investigate the physical properties of metals, non-metals and metalloids such as their melting and boiling point, thermal and electrical conductivity, ductility or malleability.
  • Investigate the uses of common elements, compounds and alloys such as copper for electrical wiring, sodium bicarbonate used in baking, or steel used in building.
  • Investigate tests used to identify metals and non-metals such as tests for gases – oxygen, hydrogen and carbon dioxide or flame tests for some metal ions.
  • Investigate how models of atomic structure have changed over time including the contributions of Dalton, Rutherford, Bohr, Thompson and Chadwick.
  • Investigate the history of the periodic table to design a timeline for the classroom.

In context

Students are required to investigate how the properties and availability of materials influence their uses. This would be a good opportunity for students to research different metals, alloys and compounds to develop a better understanding of abundance and how these materials are found in nature. Students could investigate:

  • why certain elements are found mainly as compounds in nature, such as sodium, which is found mainly as sodium chloride
  • why gold and silver are used for jewellery
  • why steel and bronze became popular alloys
  • why it took so long to discover some elements
  • how the abundance of high-grade iron ore in Australia has led to a thriving steel industry.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a persuasive text on why an element or compound’s use has changed due to evolving technology or trends.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as explicit teaching of the language of persuasion and the use of scaffolds to produce persuasive text.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Research the ‘ancient’ elements (gold, silver, iron, lead, tin, sulfur) and explain why their properties suited their function.
  • Design a periodic table of unknown elements based on their physical properties and abilities to react with hydrochloric acid.
  • Research how new technologies have filled in some of the unstable elements in periods 6 and 7 of the periodic table.
  • Investigate the relationship between element properties, technology, discovery and use.

This focus area introduces students to the physical properties of the 3 states of matter with a specific focus on the properties of water. Students learn to distinguish between atoms, mixtures and compounds and how the different types of mixtures can be separated based on their physical properties.

Key ideas

  • Water can be found as a solid, liquid and gas
  • Density
  • SI units of measurement
  • Solute, solvent and solution
  • Properties of solutions
  • Classifying matter as pure substances (compounds) and impure substances (mixtures)
  • Particle theory of matter
  • Separating mixtures using physical properties

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to observe different chemistry phenomena by planning and conducting a number of practical investigations. Students should also be given the opportunity to use their knowledge in problem-solving by identifying different solutions and strategies.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • planning an investigation to identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables when investigating the change in temperature of water as it is heated; the solubility of different substances; and the different methods used to separate mixtures
  • planning an investigation to understand the steps used to manage safety risks before, during and after an investigation
  • identify the methods and equipment needed when investigating the different methods used to separate mixtures
  • suggesting possible improvements to an investigation
  • conducting an investigation by selecting and/or assembling the correct equipment and following a planned procedure
  • processing data collected as part of investigations into density
  • analysing calculated density data and comparing it to SI units of measurement outlined in the  Science 7–10 Data Book
  • recording observations and measurements accurately during investigations.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise these concepts:

  • Practice of science using Working scientifically processes, by conducting an investigation using scientific tools and tabulating and graphing data from an investigation.
  • All objects are made of materials which have certain properties.
  • The properties of materials affect how they are used.
  • Water can exist as a solid, liquid or gas.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Measure the temperature as ice melts or water evaporates over a period of time.
  • Compare the density of water to other substances.
  • Investigate what substances are soluble in water.
  • Investigate the solubility of different solutes.
  • Investigate how temperature affects solubility.
  • Investigate the effect of salt on boiling point – 5% w/w, 10% w/w, 20% w/w, 30% w/w.
  • Investigate how to separate different types of mixtures.
  • Identify the cause-and-effect relationships involved in the cleaning of polluted water.

In context

Students model how a body of water can be polluted and then plan and conduct a practical investigation to ‘clean’ the water they have polluted. For example, students could add small pieces of plastic to represent rubbish pollution, vinegar to represent acid rain, or dirt to represent land clearing and then plan an investigation to separate some of the pollutants. This could be an opportunity for students to produce a scientific report, newspaper article or presentation on how to remove or prevent pollutants in a body of water.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds to produce a report or article, or the opportunity to plan and discuss their presentation using their home language or dialect.

This is a good opportunity for the students to learn how to conduct a second-hand research activity after researching their local water catchment area and identifying where that water comes from. Additionally, students could research what factors could contribute to a body of water becoming polluted and how that could be prevented.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate the effect of temperature on how much solute can be dissolved in water to make supersaturated solutions.
  • Investigate how solutions are used in everyday products. This can be expanded to look at the growing market of cleaning solutions that are made into solids to decrease the use of plastic consumption.
  • Investigate how an understanding of separating of mixtures is used in the dairy industry to make butter, buttermilk or cottage cheese.
  • Research how blood can be separated to make plasma, red blood cell and platelet transfusions, and why these 3 methods have been developed.

In this focus area, students continue to learn to analyse data, including using large datasets to draw evidence-based conclusions. This focus area provides a foundation for students in making evidence-based decisions and evaluating claims and content in their everyday lives, and also for students preparing for study in Stage 6 Science.

Key ideas

  • Peer review
  • Validity of secondary data and information
  • Reliability of secondary data and information
  • Scientific claims
  • Pseudoscience
  • Bias
  • Univariate data analysis
  • Bivariate data analysis
  • Causation
  • Correlation

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to conduct investigations to analyse data and information as it relates to hypothesis testing, the roles of repetition and peer review, as well as what it means for a claim to be scientifically testable. Students should examine a variety of claims for testability, determine whether online sources are valid, and communicate their arguments using evidence. Students should also use large datasets to represent and analyse data and draw evidence-based conclusions.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • problem-solving by posing questions to investigate and analyse
  • analysing data using descriptive techniques, performing a simple test to determine correlation and justifying whether the variables analysed show a causative relationship
  • communicating conclusions using scientific reasoning.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts:

  • Accuracy and precision
  • Reliability
  • Validity
  • Analysing data to identify trends, patterns and relationships
  • Communicating scientific arguments with evidence
  • Using mean, median and mode to describe data
  • Representing data in various forms, such as scatter plots, line graphs, column graphs, Frequency histograms, and box and whisker plots
  • Outliers.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Develop criteria to evaluate whether online content such as social media or advertisements are scientifically testable.
  • Plan and conduct a first-hand investigation to test an identified claim.
  • Plan and conduct an investigation to test a scientific model, theory or law, for example the law of conservation of mass; whether embankments (levees) prevent flooding; the effectiveness of natural antiseptics on inhibiting microbial growth. Evaluate whether the data collected provides support for the identified model, theory or law.
  • Investigate examples that demonstrate how data and information can be used to misinform by the way it's presented. Use a scaffold to evaluate the credibility of a source of information such as an article, blog or post.
  • Investigate examples of scientifically testable ideas, eg Ernest Rutherford testing the idea that an atom’s positive mass is spread out diffusely; Ignaz Semmelweis testing the idea that childbed fever was caused by doctors’ unclean hands; Jean-Baptiste Lamarck’s theory of evolution of acquired characteristics.

In context

Students use data to make evidence-based decisions about a familiar issue and assess the implications of these decisions. Examples of issues include greenhouse gas emissions, changes in sea temperature and sea level.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a journal article, infographic or vlog to communicate the issue, assess proposed decisions and/or solutions, and make logical, scientific evidence-based arguments and conclusions.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as pre-teaching vocabulary and scaffolds to produce a journal article or vlog.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Create a short video debunking a common myth, such as the myth that it is possible to pop popcorn with a mobile phone.
  • Access a large dataset to pose questions and hypotheses. Students analyse the data to identify trends, patterns and relationships, and justify whether relationships are causal or correlational. Students explore different ways to represent the data, draw evidence-based conclusions and communicate their findings. Examples include Global Mean Sea Level (CSIRO), Investigating radiation in the air we breathe (ANSTO) or Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (NOAA).
  • Use a rubric to evaluate a pseudoscientific claim, eg astrology, the lunar effect (the Moon’s influence on human behaviour), that GMO foods are unhealthy, the difference between chromotherapy (light) and neonatal jaundice therapy. Students could then apply this rubric to evaluate a claim of their own choosing.

This focus area develops students’ understanding of the cause and prevention of infectious and non-infectious disease, further consolidating learning about body systems and their role in coordinating responses in the human body. Students examine data on the occurrence of infectious diseases to identify trends, patterns and relationships and draw conclusions.

Key ideas

  • Homeostasis
  • Stimulus–response model
  • Infectious and non-infectious disease
  • Immune system
  • Vaccination
  • Immunisation
  • Modelling to predict spread of disease
  • Epidemiology
  • Disease-prevention strategies

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

Students should be given the opportunity to analyse data to identify trends, patterns and relationships about the cause and pattern of the spread of disease and communicate conclusions that are consistent with the data. Students should construct evidence-based arguments, for example the efficacy of vaccinations and other methods of preventing infectious and non-infectious disease.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • examining examples of scientific models that predict the spread of disease, eg online games and simulations, and analyse how these models can be used to coordinate disease-prevention measures
  • evaluating strategies used to prevent and control previous disease outbreaks and communicate strategies for future prevention, eg polio outbreaks in Australia both before and following the introduction of vaccination; Cancer Council SunSmart campaign to reduce rates of melanoma.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Cells as the basis of all living things
  • Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms
  • Classification of cells based on structures
  • Body systems coordinate to maintain a functioning organism.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Investigate how the nervous system responds to a stimulus, eg reaction time.
  • Investigate the performance and effectiveness of cleaning products such as hand wash, hand sanitiser and surface spray.
  • Model the spread of infectious disease using games or simulations.
  • Use diagrams to model feedback loops that maintain homeostasis, eg temperature control.
  • Interpret graphs to make predictions about the body’s response to stimuli and maintenance of homeostasis, eg control of blood glucose levels in a healthy person versus someone with type 2 diabetes.
  • Gather and present information about the causes of infectious and non-infectious diseases.
  • Use datasets and other sources of information to pose questions and make hypotheses about factors that contribute to infectious disease, eg compare deaths due to influenza across different countries to discuss contributing factors such as temperature, climate, socioeconomic status.
  • Investigate the cause, effects and strategies used to prevent and/or manage a non-infectious disease such as obesity or type 2 diabetes.
  • Investigate some key scientists who have contributed to our understanding of disease, such as Louis Pasteur, Albert Sabin or Françoise Barré-Sinoussi.

In context

Students investigate technological advances developed in Australia to address diseases, disorders or physical traumas in the human body.

Possible technologies to investigate could include:

  • spray-on skin to treat burns
  • the Malaria Vaccine Project (Griffith University, Qld)
  • artificial retinas created by biomedical printing press
  • stem cells to restore sight
  • contact tracing applications

This could be a good opportunity for students to develop their skills and understanding of the importance of science communication to the public and for students to produce a report, online news article or podcast episode.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds to produce a report or article as well as the provision to plan and discuss their podcast in their home language or dialect.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate a specific disease outbreak, eg Ebola in Sierra Leone (2014–2016); cholera in Haiti (Port-au-Prince, 2010); outbreak of Hendra virus in Qld and NSW (2011). Students process and present data including graphs and tables to show how data has been used to track and manage the spread of disease. Students evaluate the efficacy of measures used to manage and prevent disease and propose how new technologies such as DNA sequencing and nanotechnology could be used in future outbreaks.
  • Design an education campaign targeted towards a specific audience to prevent disease, eg a campaign to promote the HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer; a campaign aimed at reducing rates of obesity or type 2 diabetes in Australia.
  • Extend understanding of disease to investigate how diseases mutate and create new strains of the disease and how scientists work to develop new vaccinations to cover these new strains.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area extends students’ understanding of the different forms of energy and how electrical energy flows through different types of circuits. Additionally, students learn how to evaluate data so that they can make better energy choices in future.

Key ideas

  • Law of conservation of energy
  • Energy transfers
  • Energy efficiency
  • Renewable energy
  • Non-renewable energy
  • Electrical circuits
  • Ohm’s law
  • Data analysis of energy use
  • New energy sources

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to observe a number of different energy sources and undertake investigations making and comparing parallel and series circuits. Students could develop observing skills and skills in conducting investigations by selecting and using the correct equipment to construct and test a number of different series and parallel circuits. They should also be given the opportunity to develop problem-solving skills by accessing and analysing scientific data to identify trends and patterns in the use of different energy sources.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • conducting investigations by following a series of planned procedures to make different series and parallel circuits and to measure voltage and current
  • conducting investigations by following a series of planned procedures to compare the resistance of wires by their type, length or width
  • developing problem-solving skills by researching and proposing solutions on how to improve energy efficiency
  • developing problem-solving skills by researching the advantages and disadvantages of renewable and non-renewable resources to generate electricity
  • developing problem-solving skills by researching the energy star ratings of appliances and explaining and evaluating how these ratings are determined
  • developing problem-solving skills by researching and proposing how to evaluate ways to optimise current energy use.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Practice of science
  • Importance of energy
  • Different forms of energy
  • How energy is stored
  • Energy transfer
  • Collect and analyse datasets.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Conducting an experiment that demonstrates the law of conservation of energy.
  • Constructing parallel and series circuits and using the electric circuit symbols in the Science 7–10 Data Book to correctly draw the circuits.
  • Measuring and comparing voltage and current in parallel and series circuits.
  • Conducting a series of experiments to prove Ohm’s law by determining the relationship between voltage, current and resistance.
  • Using energy star ratings on a range of appliances and determining which appliance would increase or decrease energy use in the home.
  • Investigating the difference between energy consumption in a range of light bulbs such as incandescent, fluorescent, LED (light emitting diode) and CFL (compact fluorescent lamp).

In context

Students are required to evaluate the development of alternative energy sources to meet and reduce global energy demand using data, evidence and research. Students could first investigate data about global energy demand (eg whether particular countries, regions or cities have higher energy demands than others and why). Students could then explore existing or emerging alternative energy sources. They could examine alternative energy sources in different global areas. Students would use these datasets to identify trends and patterns in energy use before predicting possible solutions to reducing consumption.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a report which compares global uses of electricity and possible solutions to minimise energy consumption.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and explicit teaching of the language of judgement in order to produce a report.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Use a bicycle and modify it so that it can easily power a kettle or toaster oven or charge a mobile phone. Prototyping and modelling could be used to elaborate on different designs to make the most energy with the least effort.
  • Design an energy-efficient lighting plan for a hypothetical building, considering factors such as lighting needs, energy saving and cost-effectiveness.
  • Connect the materials and the environmental sustainability focus areas and discuss the environmental impact of energy consumption, including carbon emissions, and how choosing energy-efficient lighting can reduce this impact.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This focus area extends students’ understanding of the impact of human activity on the natural world. It provides an understanding of the concept of sustainability and the evidence used to identify the impacts of climate change and the need for alternative energy resources. This focus area provides a foundation in environmental science for all students and those preparing to study in Stage 6 Earth and Environmental Science.

Key ideas

  • Non-renewable resources
  • Sustainability
  • Climate change
  • Greenhouse effect
  • Ice core samples
  • Global emissions and atmospheric temperatures
  • Evaluating raw data
  • Changes in ocean temperatures
  • Environmental pollution
  • Recycling

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to analyse different datasets to identify trends and patterns and select suitable strategies to evaluate and propose solutions to identified problems, such as climate change, increasing carbon dioxide, warming oceans, reduction in forests and changes in ice cover.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes include:

  • Analyse data to explain the changes in atmospheric temperatures that have led to the greenhouse effect by describing trends and patterns in data, describing the relationships between variables and assessing the validity and reliability of that data.
  • Analyse data to identify changes in the levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide by describing trends and patterns in data, describing the relationships between variables and assessing the validity and reliability of that data.
  • Analyse and evaluate data obtained from satellites to determine changes in ocean temperature, sea levels, forest and ice cover by describing trends and patterns in data, describing the relationships between variables and assessing the validity and reliability of that data.
  • Analyse collected graphed data to extrapolate or interpolate to make predictions.
  • Evaluate different approaches used to solve problems by comparing alternative resource use and recycling.
  • Predict possible solutions to environmental pollution including alternative resources and recycling.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • The differences between weather and climate
  • Sources of energy
  • Global future energy needs
  • Polymers
  • Practice of science
  • Energy transfers
  • Products of combustion reactions
  • Collect and analyse datasets
  • Predictions and explanations are based on data and evidence.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Conduct a practical investigation to model the greenhouse effect that shows how more heat can be trapped if there is more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
  • Research what an ice core sample reveals about changes in atmospheric gases and analyse data collected to describe trends and patterns in the data.
  • Analyse data from satellites to compare changes in global emissions and atmospheric temperatures to draw conclusions and develop evidence-based arguments.
  • Research how Aboriginal Peoples have developed sustainable harvesting practices.
  • Research alternative and innovative ways being developed for recycling waste materials in Australia and globally, such as Sweden’s waste-to-energy program or Canada’s plastic road construction projects.

In context

Students discuss the link between human activity and one specific environmental pollution concern. Students could investigate space junk, the Pacific Ocean garbage patch, the warming of oceans, and air pollution and asthma.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a report, informative pamphlet or scientific journal article.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and provision to use their home language or dialect, and a bilingual dictionary to conduct research and produce a report or article.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate building resilient infrastructure ready to meet the challenges of extreme weather events and a changing climate.
  • Investigate alternative ways to educate the public about using renewable resources.
  • Design an alternative way to encourage more people to recycle.
  • Investigate the potential impacts of water garbage traps on a specific marine ecosystem such as the Great Barrier Reef.
  • Extend understanding of environmental pollution concerns by investigating the factors that led to the hole in the ozone layer and then how global efforts to address the issue of ozone depletion led to several key changes in human activity.

system.name: MS S5 Teaching advice for Environmental sustainability

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In this focus area, students will learn about genetics, genetic technologies and evolution. They will explore how DNA, mutations and evolution play a role in the diversity of life. This focus area provides a foundation for all students in genetic technologies and also for those students preparing for study in Stage 6 Biology.

Key ideas

  • DNA structure and function
  • History and collaboration behind the structure of DNA
  • Comparisons between genes, DNA, chromosomes and genomes
  • Genetic variation
  • Genotype and phenotype
  • Pedigrees and Punnett squares
  • Mutation
  • Genetic technologies including ethical and social considerations
  • Theory of evolution and diversity
  • Natural selection
  • Speciation and diversity
  • Geological timescales and evidence
  • Origin of species

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to process data and information. They may also extract information, using a range of sources and identifying data that supports their research question. Students should be given the opportunity to communicate their ideas and present their findings using evidence-based arguments and correct scientific language in written texts.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • processing data and information by observing different DNA models to compare genes, DNA, chromosomes and genomes
  • processing data and information from multiple sources to understand the many contributions of different scientists to our understanding of the structure and function of DNA
  • processing data and information by using Punnett squares and pedigrees to model inheritance patterns
  • communicating the structure and function of DNA using evidence-based arguments
  • processing data and information to communicate the application of genetic testing and its social, ethical and economic implications
  • evaluating evidence to support the theory of evolution and communicate how organisms have changed over time
  • processing data and information to show evidence of how organisms have changed over time using the geological timescale in the Science 7–10 Data Book.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Life cycles
  • Living things may change over millions of years in response to their environments
  • Factors that lead to a species becoming endangered or extinct
  • Non-infectious diseases
  • Data and scientific models
  • Cell structure and location of DNA
  • Body systems structure, function and disorders.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Extract DNA from strawberry or kiwi fruit.
  • Model DNA double helix using different materials.
  • Model pedigrees and Punnett squares for inheritance patterns.
  • Research causes and outcomes of DNA mutation.
  • Research different genetic technologies and how they have helped in conservation, agriculture, industry and medicine.
  • Research Aboriginal Peoples’ recordings of changes in flora and fauna including megafauna.
  • Research how the origin of species and the theory of evolution has developed and changed over time.

In context

Students are required to use an ethical framework to construct evidence-based written arguments about the implications of a genetic technology, including the ethical implications of the continued use of the HeLa stem cell line. This could include stem cell research and the use of HeLa stem cells, the use of CRISPR-Cas9 in gene therapy, or the use of transgenic species in agriculture, medicine or industry.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a persuasive text outlining the ethical and social considerations of a specific genetic technology that has evolved because of the HeLa stem cells and whether they should still be used.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as provision to use their home language or dialect and a bilingual dictionary to conduct research. They may also require the explicit teaching of persuasive language and the use of scaffolds to produce a persuasive text.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate a particular genetic technology for a specific purpose and present findings as a journal article, video news piece or brochure.
  • Research the history of Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa stem cells and how they have helped stem cell research.
  • Make a timeline poster showing the evolution of scientific knowledge of the structure of DNA.
  • Develop inquiry question(s) relating to stem cells, then research and present the information for a specific audience.

This focus area expands students’ understanding of properties of matter, patterns and relationships in the periodic table, including chemical bonding, and the use of materials based on their properties. Students learn organic chemistry and develop an understanding of where fuels and plastics come from. Students evaluate the impact of the extraction and use of different minerals and resources.

Key ideas

  • Uses of minerals and resources in Australia
  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ use of minerals and resources
  • Noble gas configuration
  • Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds
  • Chemical formula of common ionic and covalent molecules
  • IUPAC naming conventions – alkanes
  • Separation and uses of hydrocarbons from crude oil
  • Complete and incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons
  • Properties of plastics, including biodegradability

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to design and collect valid and reliable secondary data and use problem-solving strategies to assess the impact of the extraction and use of a variety of resources, including the use of hydrocarbons and other alternatives. Students should be given the opportunity to communicate as they present scientific arguments using evidence and correct scientific terminology. Students should design safe, ethical, valid and reliable investigations.

Additional examples of how to embed Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • problem-solving by selecting suitable strategies and evaluating proposed solutions to identified problems
  • collecting data and developing further questions that could be investigated as part of a physical survey of a local area.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • Physical and chemical properties of matter
  • Separation of mixtures based on physical properties
  • Particle theory of matter
  • Atomic structure
  • How to determine the number of electrons in the outer shell of an atom
  • Patterns and relationships in the periodic table
  • Indicators of a chemical change
  • Word equations to describe a chemical reaction.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Investigate the extraction, preparation or use of a mineral or resource of importance to their local area.
  • Investigate how Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples access and use the environment when preparing tools.
  • Construct models to describe the formation of cations and anions.
  • Compare the amount of energy released using different hydrocarbons, eg using spirit burners containing ethanol, propan-1-ol, and butan-1-ol to heat water and measure the increase in temperature using secondary data to graph the amount of heat energy released and drawing conclusions about the length of the hydrocarbon chain and amount of heat energy released.
  • Design and conduct an investigation to determine the physical properties and biodegradability of plastics and plastic alternatives.
  • Investigate the uses of hydrocarbon compounds from pre-industrialisation and post-industrialisation, up to the rise of the plastic industry, to develop an understanding of the importance of using alternative materials to plastics.

In context

Students are required to assess the environmental impacts of materials that are being used as an alternative to those derived from crude oil. For example, research the reason(s) behind the banning microbeads in personal rinse-off products such as shampoo and draw evidence-based conclusions about the impact this has had on the environment.

Students could conduct an investigation to assess the environmental impact of changing from takeaway plastic cutlery to wood/paper alternatives, the banning of single-use plastic bags, or the replacement of plastic straws with paper ones.

This could be an opportunity for students to construct an educational campaign using different media to communicate the effect of an identified issue. Students could also write a persuasive letter about an identified issue and suggest solutions.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as pre-teaching vocabulary and scaffolds to produce an educational campaign or persuasive letter.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions for depth studies.

  • Investigate the repurposing of mining and tailing waste products, examining the associated processes and resulting products, and assessing the economic and environmental viability of these industrial activities.
  • Investigate the use of natural materials, eg traditional fibres as a replacement for synthetic materials.
  • Extend students’ understanding and investigate alternative fuel sources such as biofuels and assess the efficiency of these fuels compared to traditional octane-based fuel.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In this focus area, students learn the law of conservation of mass and that it guides the process of balancing chemical equations. Students investigate types of chemical and nuclear reactions and how the rate of a chemical reaction can be determined, measured and manipulated. This focus area provides a foundation for all students in Chemistry and also for those preparing for study in Stage 6 Chemistry.

Key ideas

  • Law of conservation of mass
  • Chemical formulas
  • Balanced chemical equations
  • Synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions
  • pH and pH indicators
  • Factors affecting rates of reaction
  • Nuclear decay reactions
  • Half-life
  • Radioisotopes

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to observe different chemical reactions in practical investigations that they have planned themselves. Students should develop skills in questioning and predicting by writing and testing a hypothesis to measure the rate of chemical reactions as well as predicting precipitations in a reaction between 2 ionic solutions.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • conducting investigations to measure pH changes in neutralisation reactions
  • processing and analysing data about the half-life of various isotopes and implications for their uses.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise the following concepts.

  • All objects are made of materials which have certain properties
  • Identifying indicators of a chemical change
  • Law of conservation of energy
  • How to write a chemical formula
  • States of matter
  • Atomic structure and numbers of sub-atomic particles
  • Ionic compounds
  • Safety considerations in a chemical reaction.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Law of conservation of mass precipitation reaction between barium nitrate and sodium sulfate to produce the barium sulfate precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate. The reaction can be done on a set of digital scales. The formation of the white BaSO4 precipitate provides an indicator that a reaction has taken place. The total mass of the reaction will not change. (Note: barium nitrate is slightly toxic, may be harmful if swallowed, causes eye irritation and is harmful if inhaled.)
  • Synthesis reactions could include Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s).
  • Decomposition reactions could include CuCO3(s) → CuO(s) + CO2(g). This could also be a good opportunity to test the production of CO2 by bubbling it through limewater.
  • Single displacement reaction: Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → 2Ag(s) + Cu(NO3)2(aq). (Note: silver nitrate is toxic and corrosive to eyes and skin. Silver residue should be disposed of in a silver waste container.)
  • Double displacement reactions include Fe(NO3)3(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s) + 3NaNO3(aq) / HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(s) + H2O(l).
  • Investigate the pH change of neutralisation reactions by using acid-base indicators as listed in the Science 7–10 Data Book to determine the end point of the reaction.

In context

Students are required to investigate a chemical or nuclear reaction used in industry to produce an important product. Students research or connect to a local industry and investigate the various chemicals manufactured at plants across Australia. Possible chemicals to investigate include chlor-alkali, methanol, polymers, wastewater treatment solutions or any other industrial processes on a local, national or global level, which are of interest to students. Students investigate the industrial chemical reaction, reaction conditions, product(s) and their importance to society, and environmental and safety considerations.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a research report, a scientific journal article or a factual description.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and provision to use their home language or dialect and a bilingual dictionary to conduct research and produce a report, article or description.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions of depth studies.

  • Investigate chemical reactions that occur in everyday life.
  • Investigate an industrial process and the conditions that are manipulated to change the rate of the reaction to increase the yield. Industrial processes could include the Haber process.
  • Connect understanding of nuclear reactions and the Energy focus area to investigate the potential of nuclear energy as a replacement energy source.
  • Extend understanding of the impact of nuclear reactions by investigating nuclear reactions with harmful intentions such as the bombing of Hiroshima.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
In this focus area, students learn key concepts related to waves and motion, and the application of these concepts. Students differentiate between mechanical and electromagnetic (EM) waves, analyse waves, and learn to understand wave behaviours. Students conduct investigations to determine relationships between distance, time, speed, force, mass and acceleration. They apply Newton's laws of motion and use mathematical representations to quantitatively relate motion variables. This focus area provides a foundation for all students in waves and motion and also for those preparing for study in Stage 6 Physics.

Key ideas

  • Waves transfer energy
  • Mechanical waves need a medium
  • Transverse waves
  • Longitudinal waves
  • Behaviour of light waves: reflection, refraction, absorption and diffraction
  • SI units for time, distance, speed, mass, acceleration, force and energy
  • Motion: displacement versus distance
  • Scalar versus vector measurements
  • Magnitude and direction
  • Distance travelled calculated from velocity and time graphs
  • Newton’s laws of motion

Skills

Working scientifically processes which are most relevant for the intended learning have been identified for each focus area.

In this focus area, students should be given the opportunity to develop their skills in conducting investigations and processing data and information.

Additional examples of how to embed the Working scientifically processes in this focus area include:

  • modelling to show how energy is transferred through different mediums
  • analysing and extracting data from a wide range of reliable resources to compare the different uses of EM waves and examine how sound waves are used in medical diagnosis
  • modelling skills to compare transverse and longitudinal waves
  • extracting data from a range of reliable resources to look at the different materials and designs used by Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples to make cultural instruments for communication
  • planning safe and valid experiments to investigate the properties of light including reflection, refraction, absorbing and scattering
  • modelling force diagrams showing displacement versus distance travelled
  • processing data and information by using SI units to calculate force, distance, time, speed, displacement, acceleration, velocity and mass. Students make these calculations by determining the correct formula to use based on information in the questions.

Background knowledge

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area. Students who need extra support should have opportunities to revise these concepts:

  • objects move in different ways depending on what is done to them
  • practice of science
  • types of forces
  • balanced and unbalanced forces
  • simple machines
  • scientific models
  • gravity as a force
  • performing calculations to solve for unknowns
  • drawing and analysing graphs.

Investigations

The following investigations may engage students’ interest and further develop the targeted Working scientifically skills.

  • Investigate how waves move energy.
  • Place light waves through different mediums, eg glass, water, opaque plastic.
  • Use tuning forks to change and measure the amplitude and frequency of sound waves to see how this affects pitch and volume.
  • Use light ray boxes and mirrors to learn about absorption, reflection, refraction and scattering of light waves.
  • Use different shaped lenses to show how the focal point can be changed and how glasses correct vision problems.
  • Investigate and compare walking and running speeds over the same distance to collect and analyse a class dataset.
  • Use toy cars and ramps to show the relationship between distance, time and speed.
  • Use balls of the same size but different masses to show how mass does not affect acceleration due to gravity.
  • Investigate how mass affects acceleration using pulleys, different masses, ticker timers or light gates.

In context

Students are required to structure an argument to analyse how waves and motion have changed society. Students could analyse how our understanding of these concepts has changed society with inventions such as glasses, hearing aids, planes, helicopters, earbuds and optical fibres.

This could be an opportunity for students to produce a scientific newspaper article depicting the history of telescopes and how our knowledge of space has evolved to justify additional funding for space agencies.

Students learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) may require support such as scaffolds and explicit teaching of the language of evaluation to produce a scientific newspaper article.

Suggested depth study

Depth studies are an opportunity for students to pursue an area of strength or interest. The following are suggestions of depth studies.

  • Build a working speaker out of paper.
  • Design soundproof material made from recycled material.
  • Analyse people’s voices by their digital sound waves.
  • Investigate how the length of a guitar string affects frequency.
  • Extend understanding of stars to investigate how the surface temperature and/or chemical makeup of stars is identified using spectroscopy.

web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Content
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Assessment is used to analyse and interpret the knowledge, understanding and skills that students demonstrate throughout the learning process. Assessment provides information about student learning and achievement at a point in time and the progress students have made.

Assessment is most effective when it is an integral part of teaching and learning. The primary role of assessment is to identify where students are in their learning so that teaching can be adapted to target student needs, and progress can be monitored over time.

Schools use syllabuses, assessment and reporting materials and Assessment Certification and Examination (ACE) requirements to develop school-based assessment programs.

Assessment involves:

  •  identifying where students are in their learning
  •  ongoing monitoring of student progress in relation to the syllabus
  •  providing feedback about student progress to determine the next steps in learning.

Effective school-based assessment:

  • enables students to demonstrate what they know, understand and can do
  • is inclusive of, and accessible for, all students
  • is valid: there is clear alignment between the syllabus, the assessment activity and the criteria used to assess
  • identifies strengths, misunderstandings and skills not yet mastered
  • enables timely and relevant feedback about learning progress
  • provides opportunities for students to reflect on feedback
  • is regular, purposeful and integrated throughout teaching and learning
  • informs goal setting for learning and teaching.

Teachers should evaluate the effectiveness of their assessment approaches regularly to ensure they are fit for purpose. Reviewing student work in relation to assessment activities can provide useful information for decision-making.

Decisions teachers make about teaching, learning and assessment include:

  • what outcomes will be assessed in relation to the content that has been taught
  • why assessment will occur at a point in time and for what purpose
  • how information about student learning will be gathered and what approach will be used
  • how the information will be used, including to provide feedback, and to determine student progress and achievement
  • what next steps will inform future teaching and learning.

Standards-referenced assessment

Standards-referenced assessment refers to the process of interpreting information about student learning in relation to standards. It is used to compare student performance to a standard with objective criteria rather than to the performance of other students. Standards-referenced assessment can provide meaningful feedback about student achievement and support consistent assessment and reporting.

What are standards?

A standards-referenced approach is used to assess and report student achievement in NSW. This approach comprises 2 components:

  • syllabus outcomes and content describe what students are expected to learn
  • how well students demonstrate achievement is described in performance standards such as the Common Grade Scale.

Syllabus outcomes are used by teachers to:

  • plan and develop learning and assessment opportunities in relation to content
  • assess student progress and achievement in relation to intended learning
  • report student progress and achievement at key points in time.

Performance standards used to report student achievement in NSW include:

  • Common Grade Scale (Years 1 to 10)
  • Stage 5 Course Performance Descriptors (end of Year 10)
  • Common Grade Scale for preliminary courses (Year 11)
  • HSC Performance Band Descriptions (Year 12)
  • achievement level descriptions (Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1, and Numeracy).

It is not a requirement for student reports in Early Stage 1 to refer to a performance standard such as a grade scale. More information on standards-referenced reporting is available in Reporting and using grades.

Inclusive assessment

Approaches to assessment should be inclusive of all students. Assessment design should consider the ways students engage in the activity, how information is presented and accessed, and the different ways that students can demonstrate their understanding. Inclusive assessment means ensuring all students are able to demonstrate their learning.

Inclusive assessment considers the following:

  • How students engage:
    • developing accessible learning goals and criteria
    • integrating student choice, for example allowing students to choose topics or contexts in which they demonstrate learning
    • simulating real-life contexts that have explicit relevance to students.
  • How information is presented and accessed, including:
    • resources and/or stimulus material that is presented across a range of modes and that include accessibility options
    • both digital and non-digital resources.
  • How students respond:
    • using self-paced activities that support students to demonstrate learning without time constraints
    • providing opportunities for students to make choices about how they communicate their learning
    • providing opportunities to challenge and/or extend students within their level of understanding.

Adjustments for students with disability

It is a requirement under the Disability Standards for Education 2005 for schools to ensure that assessment tasks are accessible to students with disability. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access assessment activities and tasks and to demonstrate their learning. In some cases, this may mean providing an alternative assessment activity. Schools are responsible for any decisions made at school level to offer adjustments to assessment activities and tasks, including in-school tests. Decisions regarding adjustments should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

  • Assessment in Stage 6

Checking grades involves reviewing the history of grades allocated by a school to analyse patterns and clarify grading decisions.

When making comparisons, teachers should ensure their grading decisions are based on all available assessment information referenced by relevant grade scales or performance descriptors and published standards.

Schools can use the Grade History Function in Schools Online or the Results Analysis Package to view the grades they have allocated in each course.

Schools can monitor their grade patterns by comparing them to other available data about the performance of students at their school. This will enable schools to have confidence that the grades they intend to allocate are consistent with what they expected from a particular cohort or group of students completing a course.

Principals are accountable for the pattern of grades allocated by their school at the end of Stage 5 and Year 11 courses (except Life Skills and VET) and Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC. Principals (or their delegates) need to confirm that grades are consistent with published standards when they are submitted.
